initial_observation.encounter_context: presented to the plastic surgery clinic
initial_observation.chief_complaint: a persistent swelling localised to the right posterior scalp associated with pruritus
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: persistent swelling in right posterior scalp with pruritus for approximately 4 months, progressive enlargement with intermittent discomfort, no bleeding, weight loss, night sweats or fever; dermatological examination revealed two right parieto-occipital scalp lesions: a 12 mm subcutaneous, mobile, tender cystic lesion with intact skin and an 11 mm erythematous lesion with irregular borders and brown discolouration
presenting_symptoms: persistent swelling localised to the right posterior scalp

evidence_items.source_text: Sonographic evaluation of the scalp revealed two adjacent hypoechoic lesions located in the parietal region, with the largest measuring 10×8 mm, resembling epidermoid cysts.

An initial excisional biopsy of the second lesion was performed under local anaesthesia and submitted for histopathological analysis. The biopsy revealed a basaloid cutaneous lesion consistent with adenoid cystic carcinoma, as observed in the H&E histological section (figure 1). Immunohistochemistry was performed, revealing that the lesion exhibited patchy infiltrates positively staining for epithelial membrane antigen, specifically staining the apical aspect of the pseudo glandular cyst (figure 2A). Additionally, there was diffuse positive staining for pan-cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) (figure 2B). These findings, along with previous imaging, supported the diagnosis of PCACC and were crucial in distinguishing this lesion from other similar neoplastic processes.
The PET-CT scan revealed the absence of fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake or hypermetabolic activity, with normal physiological FDG distribution in the lymph nodes, organs and bone marrow.

Under local anaesthesia, the two lesions were completely excised surgically. Subsequent reconstruction of the operative site involved the use of a local flap using adjacent skin to reconstruct and fill the defect created by the surgical excision on the scalp. A rotational flap was used, repositioning surrounding scalp tissue in an arc to effectively cover the excision site.
Histopathological examination of the excised tissue confirmed the diagnosis of PCACC and demonstrated clear surgical margins.
